#773. ‘I Didn’t Want to Become Fat, Bloated, Naked Elvis’: Why KISS Called It Quits on Touring (And What They’re Up to Now)

Gene Simmons and Paul Stanley are gearing up for the release of the KISS: End of the Road documentary.

It’s been nearly three years since KISS played its last concert as a touring act — and in makeup. Now the group is giving fans a look behind the scenes of its End of the Road World Tour, a globe-spanning farewell trek that was bumpier than the KISS camp let on. Explore Kiss See latest videos, charts and news

The revealing KISS: End of the Road documentary drops Nov. 19 via KISSOnline.com, where it will be available for seven days before moving on to other platforms. The band will preview the film during its KISS Kruise: Land-Locked in Vegas convention Nov. 13-15 at the Virgin Hotel in Las Vegas, where it will also play acoustic and electric concerts and host a tribute to late original guitarist Ace Frehley, who passed away in October 2025 at the age of 74. Related Aria Vega Wins Best New Artist at the 2026 Latin Grammys: 'Dreams Know No Fear' On Winning First Latin Grammy, Camila Fernández Thanks Expectant Baby for 'Strength to be Here' 50 Cent Trolls Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Affair With 'P.I.M.P.' Music Video AI Deepfake: 'Jensen Don't Sweat It'

KISS’ recent spate of activity also includes the release of box sets celebrating the 50th anniversary of the group’s fifth studio album, Rock and Roll Over, which spent 45 weeks on the Billboard 200 and peaked at No. 11 in 1976. At the same time, the KISS Army is awaiting an avatar show that’s been in the works for several years, as well as a biopic that’s also in process.

“It’s as it should be,” the group’s Paul Stanley tells Billboard via Zoom about KISS’ continuing life after reaching the End of the Road. “KISS is larger than life, and KISS isn’t about the four individuals. It’s about the four persons, the four characters. It’s a timeless thing, so I totally get those four going on. I can get older, but he [Stanley’s Starchild character] won’t.”

Gene Simmons, whom Stanley founded KISS with during 1973 in New York, adds that, “We’ve seen bands that wait too long to get off the road and it’s sad. I didn’t want to become fat, bloated, naked Elvis on the bathroom floor. So you have to know when to get off the stage as KISS. But that doesn’t mean (the band) has to end.”

The nearly two-and-a-half-hour KISS: End of the Road film shows in intimate detail that the conclusion of that phase of the band’s career was emotional, triumphant and trying.

Directed by DJ Viola, who also helmed the 2021 A&E documentary KISStory, the chronicle focuses on the final 2023 leg of the pandemic-interrupted End of the Road World Tour, which started in South America and played North America, Europe and Australia before wrapping up with homecoming performances Dec. 1-2 at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Noting that KISStory was “what we call a ‘womb-to-tomb’ documentary,” Viola tells Billboard, “I wanted End of the Road to be almost the antithesis of that approach. Rather than having the guys tell us what happened, I wanted audiences to experience it as it was happening, from the first of their final 50 shows all the way to Madison Square Garden.” He and his crew became embedded flies on the wall during the trek, capturing planning meetings, backstage intrigue and plenty of onstage highlights, as well as interviews with band members, manager Doc McGhee, Simmons’ and Stanley’s wives and others.

“For 50 years,” Viola notes, “KISS has been protective of what happens behind the curtain. Everyone says they want to show the ‘warts and all,’ but very few actually mean it. This time, the band opened that curtain completely. What you discover is that beneath all the makeup, pyro and spectacle is an unwavering commitment to giving their fans the greatest show possible. After 50 years, that dedication hasn’t diminished one bit.”

There are warts aplenty, too, including: production difficulties early on that created significant tension in the touring party; Simmons being briefly incapacitated by dehydration during a concert in Brazil; and Stanley suffering from a severe flu that led to the cancellation of nine shows and put the last stretch of the tour in jeopardy. There are touching scenes as well, with the band and those around them talking about reaching the end of touring life. Stanley and Simmons both choke up during the final concert while talking from the stage about their parents and growing up in New York, and Simmons even shoos the camera crew away as he and Stanley exchange sentiments during that night’s sound check.

The film ends with the two men meeting, post-tour, for a convivial conversation at a deli in Bel Air, Calif.

“The trick to being unobtrusive in documentary filmmaking is to be ubiquitous,” Viola says. “You have to be there for the dullest moments as well as the most exciting ones…. The more you’re around, the more people stop thinking about the camera. Eventually, you’re just another person in the room. You have to become part of the team while remaining as invisible as possible. It’s a strange balance, but that’s where the best moments come from.”

He adds that, “The trust we’d established during KISStory was essential. KISS allowed me into virtually every corner of their world, from rehearsals and travel to putting on their makeup, standing onstage during the shows and being there afterward when the makeup came off and they dissected the night’s performance. They knew I wasn’t there to manufacture controversy. I was there to authentically capture what was happening, good or bad.”

Stanley says the band was not bothered by the constant camera presence, explaining that at this point, he and Simmons are more comfortable letting fans inside aspects of KISS that were previously kept under wraps — and deliberately so.

“It’s more appropriate to do now,” he says. “It’s famously remembered that for the early years of the band, nobody ever saw us without makeup and that was part of the mystique, part of building this larger-than-life persona. At this point, it’s interesting to let people go behind it and in some ways, it makes it bigger because it’s such a Herculean effort to do what we’ve done. To have a band go on stage 50 years later and people go, ‘They look the same as they did,’ well, that doesn’t happen by chance. It’s all very encompassing, and always has been…. I think people can appreciate that now and realize that there’s a real person behind Superman with a Marshall amp.”

The End of the Road film nods to the past with historical footage, and it also provides a glimpse into the future by showing the group working with Sweden’s Pophouse Entertainment — which acquired KISS’ catalog and trademarks for a reported $300 million during 2024 — on the digital avatar show, which was previewed at the final Madison Square Garden date. “They’re great new partners,” Simmons says. “They’re infusing so much money into KISS; you’re gonna have theme parks and cartoons and movies…just some amazing stuff coming. They’re very cognizant of the fact that the same-old isn’t the way to do it… and want to make it easier for fans who want to control the content.”

The KISS avatar show is still a work in progress, but Simmons predicts that it will arrive “in the next year to two years, at a place that is soon to be announced. They’re really putting a lot of effort  into it.” Stanley notes that “it’s far more complicated than I certainly anticipated. It’s quite complex. But the rewards are that much greater, too.” And he clarifies that it will likely be something different from what’s expected.

“The idea was never to replicate a concert. That’s not what this is about,” Stanley says. “It’s to create an experience and almost make us your tour guides into something unworldly, and yet totally based in the music. And the idea was never to do something that was appealing exclusively to a KISS fan; we wanted to create a must-see, so to speak, regardless of your taste in music. That’s what we’re creating.”

The KISS biopic is also moving forward, with Joseph McGinty “McG” Nichol directing and casting. “Anybody who’s ever been involved in film knows you can get old waiting for a film to get made,” Stanley says. “It’s still in motion, and that’s all I can say. It’s very slow going; you can rush something out but, frankly, I love being in a position where if we can’t do a film that I’m proud of, I don’t need to do a film. It just doesn’t matter that much. It would be a nice feather in the cap, but it better be a good-looking feather or I don’t want it.”

Simmons and Stanley may have more to reveal at the KISS Kruise. Both have been preparing for the band’s performances as well as the Frehley tribute, an all-star event during which Frehley’s band will back a roster of guests, including alumnus guitarist Bruce Kulick.

The Rock and Roll Over sets, meanwhile, feature a new mix by original album producer Eddie Kramer, along with outtakes, alternative mixes, demos and a live 1977 performance from Japan. “To have Eddie Kramer go in and rethink things was great,” Stanley says. “And I’m certainly open to looking into other people working on other albums and go in and reimagine them, rebirth them. I’m always in favor of making something better when it’s possible.”

Both men have their own projects as well: Simmons has dates booked into 2027 with his solo band and produced the film Deep Water; Stanley is actively painting “four or five days a week” and says his band Soul Station “will get back up and running soon.”

Meanwhile, KISS is also approaching the one-year anniversary (Dec. 7) of its Kennedy Center Honor — and also potentially being part of the last class to be feted in the actual venue, whose main building is closed to the public amid disputes over U.S. President Donald Trump’s efforts to rename and remodel the historic venue. (This year’s Honors will be presented at the Capital One Arena in Washington, D.C.)

None of that has affected the way Simmons and Stanley view their honor, however.

“All things must pass; nothing lasts forever,” Simmons notes. “I remember when Elvis (Presley) was invited by President Nixon to receive some kind of awards and stuff; I thought, ‘Cool.’ Do I agree with the politics of President Nixon? No, but he’s the duly elected president. President Trump is our president, and that’s it. What you think politically, that’s for the ballot box.”

Stanley adds that, “I don’t believe anyone ever went to any of the (honorees) and said, ‘Who did you vote for?’ That’s supposed to be a non-issue. For me, getting it was just part of the trifecta, so to speak. We got the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. We got the Songwriters Hall of Fame, and then to get the Kennedy Center Honor…. I’m at a point in my life now where it really comes down to, if you love me, let me know. Don’t put it in an obituary or my eulogy. If there’s an accolade you want to give me, I’m here.”

#772. Life With Derek Star Says Actors “Leaned Into” Stepsibling Romance

Life With Derek’s Michael Seater revealed that he and costar Ashley Leggat were not only aware of romance rumors between their stepsibling characters, but they “leaned into” it on screen.

Nearly 15 years after Life With Derek concluded, the actor behind the titular Derek Venturi in show admitted he and onscreen stepsister Ashley Leggat—a.k.a. Casey McDonald—leaned into their characters’ flirty tension while filming the blended family comedy.

“We had an undeniable chemistry that the fans loved,” Seater recalled during a recent appearance on the Back to the Best podcast. “Enemies to lovers? Whatever the trope is? So, fans wanted that and we were like, ‘Well they’re step siblings so technically…’”

Seater and Leggat played not only stepsiblings, but characters who were always at odds with each other. However, while the Canadian sitcom was airing—it aired from 2005 to 2009 on the Family Channel in Canada in the Disney Channel in the U.S. before ending with a 2010 movie—many fans picked up on how the constant fire between their characters could easily burn into a romance.

And the actors didn’t let that speculation go unnoticed.

“In these early days of the internet, our producers don’t know there’s like forums online where people are talking but we do,” the 39-year-old explained. “So, we saw that the fans were talking about it. We knew that the fans liked it, so we leaned into it without letting the writers or producers know that we were leaning into it.”

And while Seater and Leggat, 40, were never actually romantically involved on the show, the showrunners and writers had to step in to keep them apart. As he shared of one take, “We’d be like sitting on a couch and they’d be like, ‘Can you maybe separate yourselves a little on the couch?’”

Of course, Seater stressed that while he loved the ‘will they, won’t they?’ that existed between Derek and Casey, the duo didn’t want the stepsiblings to canonically be together.

“The thing is, won’t they,” Seater continued, “but we’d tease them a little.”

Case in point: Remember that final scene in the finale where Derek appears to seduce Casey by emphasizing their stepsibling status? Seater teased, “I know what I’m doing there.”

Behind the camera, however, Seater and Leggat—who reprised their roles in the 2023 TV movie Life with Luca—have never been anything but great friends and scene partners.

“Ashley’s always my favorite scene partner honestly because I could always do anything,” he mused. “You felt so safe. In comedy, you want to be able to try stuff and play around and it’s not always going to land and if you have a scene partner that’s like, ‘Ew I don’t know about that. That wasn’t great.’ It makes you afraid to try things. It makes you self-conscious.”

As he put it, “We just always had each other’s backs and we were always just going with it.”

For more costars who never actually dated, keep reading...

The Anyone But You costars may have found love onscreen, but that's where it stayed. Despite the onslaught of dating rumors amid their 2023 press tour, the pair emphasized that their relationship was strictly platonic.

"The two things that you have to sell a rom-com are fun and chemistry," Powell told the New York Times in April 2024. "Sydney and I have a ton of fun together, and we have a ton of effortless chemistry. That's people wanting what's on the screen off the screen, and sometimes you just have to lean into it a bit—and it worked wonderfully. Sydney is very smart."

Meanwhile, Sweeney—who was engaged to businessman Jonathan Davino at the time, though they split in March 2025 after seven years together—asserted that she and Powell didn't play up their chemistry ahead of the rom-com's release.

"Honestly, the press did it themselves. There was no leaning in, per se," she told Variety in October 2025. "Truly, the tabloids and journalists just created it and kept going."

"Glen and I genuinely care for each other and have a love and respect for one another," the actress emphasized. "I love being with him. And I think people just truly saw a really beautiful pairing."

Hermione Granger and Draco Malfoy?! If Watson had it her way, the Harry Potter franchise would have had a Hogwarts House-crossed romance going down off-screen. The actress has admitted to nursing a serious crush on her bleached blonde costar.During the Harry Potter 20th anniversary special, Watson shared that as a child she "fell in love" with Felton while on the set of their first film together, Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone. "I used to come in every day and look for his number on the call sheet, it was No. 7, and if his name was on the call sheet, it was an extra exciting day," she said during the reunion. "He was three years above me and so for him he was like, 'You're like my little sister.'"Shortly after the special premiered, fans of the series quickly took to the Internet to share their wish for the longtime friends to become something more.However, in an interview with British Vogue, Watson addressed the online reaction and put any potential dating rumors to rest. "We speak most weeks," she said, "and we just think it's sweet."

The one where Ross and Rachel were almost each other's lobsters in real-life.During HBO Max's Friends reunion, Aniston and Schwimmer—who played one of TV's most beloved couples—explained that art reflected real life a bit during the show's first season. "At some point, we were both crushing hard on each other, but it was like two ships passing because one of us was always in a relationship, and we never crossed that boundary," Schwimmer said. "We respected that."Aniston added, "Honestly, I remember saying one time to David, 'It's going to be such a bummer if the first time you and I actually kiss is going to be on national television.' And sure enough, the first time we kissed was in that coffee shop."So, instead of having a romance IRL, she explained that they "just channeled all of our adoration and love for each other into Ross and Rachel."

Arguably one of the most iconic pairings in movie history, fans have shipped Leo and Kate together since 1996's Titanic (even though she didn't make room for him on that door). Still, they never let go of their friendship, with Winslet telling The Guardian that they are "bonded for life." From walking the red carpet together at the 1998 Golden Globes to watching DiCaprio blow kisses to Winslet during her emotional 2009 Golden Globes speech, it's so evident that the feelings between the besties have only continued to grow over the past two decades, iceberg be damned.

The unexpected pairing's chemistry in 2019's A Star Is Born and its ensuing press tour made fans blind to the fact that the actor was dating Irina Shayk and the "Bad Romance" singer was engaged to Christian Carano at the time.Still, it was clear that the costars had a close bond, with Gaga revealing that she had an "instant connection" with Cooper that came "the second that I saw him."Of course, that closeness was on full display when the pair took to the Oscars stage in 2019, hand-in-hand, to perform their Best Song-winning number, "Shallow," just days after Gaga ended her engagement.

#770. AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage

Scientists at Stanford Medicine have identified a naturally occurring molecule that could lead to a new generation of weight loss medications. Early animal experiments suggest that it can suppress appetite and promote fat loss much like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, while potentially avoiding some of the drug's troublesome side effects.

The molecule, known as BRP, works differently from existing treatments. Rather than affecting several organs throughout the body, it appears to act more selectively on a part of the brain responsible for controlling hunger and metabolism. This more focused approach could eventually help people lose weight without experiencing problems such as nausea, constipation, or substantial muscle loss.

Researchers discovered BRP with the help of artificial intelligence, which allowed them to search through thousands of possible biological compounds. The findings were promising enough that the scientists began preparing for the next major step: determining whether the molecule is safe and effective in humans.

"The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues," said assistant professor of pathology Katrin Svensson, PhD. "That's why Ozempic has widespread effects including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism."

The hypothalamus is a small but essential region deep within the brain. Among its many responsibilities, it helps regulate hunger, energy use, body temperature, and other functions needed to maintain the body's internal balance. Because it plays such a central role in appetite, it is an important target for researchers developing obesity treatments.

Semaglutide works by imitating a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 1, or GLP-1. This hormone helps regulate blood sugar and signals that influence hunger and feelings of fullness. However, GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout several parts of the body, which helps explain why medications that activate them can produce effects beyond appetite suppression.

BRP appears to take another route. Although it influences some of the same broad metabolic functions as semaglutide, it activates different populations of brain cells. Scientists believe this distinction could make it possible to control hunger more precisely while reducing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

Svensson, who served as senior author of the study, published in Nature, has also cofounded a company to advance BRP toward human clinical trials. The research was led by senior research scientist Laetitia Coassolo, PhD.

How Artificial Intelligence Uncovered a Hidden Molecule

Finding BRP required solving a problem that has long complicated the search for new hormones. The human body produces enormous numbers of small protein fragments, but only a fraction have important biological functions. Identifying the ones that influence appetite or metabolism can be extremely difficult.

Many hormones begin as larger, inactive proteins known as prohormones. Specialized enzymes cut these proteins into smaller pieces called peptides. Some of those peptides become chemical messengers that help coordinate processes such as energy metabolism, appetite, and organ function.

A single prohormone can be cut in several different places, potentially producing numerous peptides with distinct effects. The challenge is determining which fragments are biologically useful and which are simply leftovers from normal protein processing. The important peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) can be difficult to distinguish from the much larger collection of ordinary protein fragments.

Traditional approaches often involve extracting proteins from biological tissues and analyzing them with techniques such as mass spectrometry. This method identifies molecules by measuring characteristics related to their mass, but the sheer number of possible peptides makes searching for new hormones a demanding process.

The Stanford team decided to approach the problem differently. They concentrated on an enzyme called prohormone convertase 1/3, which cuts prohormones at particular amino acid sequences and has previously been linked to human obesity. Amino acids are the molecular building blocks of proteins, and their arrangement helps determine where enzymes can cut them.

One of the hormones produced through this process is GLP-1, the same hormone whose effects semaglutide mimics. The researchers reasoned that other peptides generated through similar processing might also help regulate appetite and energy use.

AI Searches 20,000 Human Genes for New Hormones

To accelerate the search, the scientists created a computer algorithm called Peptide Predictor. Instead of physically isolating and examining hundreds of thousands of peptides, the program analyzed the roughly 20,000 genes that encode human proteins, looking for sequences where the enzyme was likely to make cuts.

The team then refined the results by concentrating on genes associated with proteins released outside cells, a common characteristic of hormones. They also required each candidate protein to contain at least four potential cutting sites.

These filters reduced an enormous collection of possibilities to 373 prohormones, making experimental testing much more practical.

"The algorithm was absolutely key to our findings," Svensson said.

Peptide Predictor estimated that the enzyme could produce 2,683 distinct peptides from those 373 proteins. From this collection, Svensson and Coassolo selected candidates that appeared particularly likely to influence brain activity.

The researchers eventually tested 100 peptides, including GLP-1, using nerve cells grown in the laboratory. Their goal was to find substances capable of stimulating neuronal activity, an early indication that a peptide might influence important brain processes.

A Tiny Peptide Produces a Surprising Result

GLP-1 performed strongly in the laboratory tests, increasing neuronal activity to three times the level observed in untreated control cells.

One previously unrecognized peptide, however, produced an even more striking response. Consisting of just 12 amino acids, it increased neuronal activity tenfold compared with the controls.

The researchers named the molecule BRP after the larger protein from which it originates, BPM/retinoic acid inducible neural specific 2, or BRINP2 (BRINP2-related-peptide).

That unusually powerful response made BRP a promising candidate for further investigation. The next question was whether stimulating laboratory-grown brain cells would translate into meaningful changes in appetite and body weight in living animals.

Food Intake Drops by Up to 50% in Animal Experiments

The team tested BRP in lean mice and minipigs (which more closely mirror human metabolism and eating patterns than mice do). Before the animals were fed, researchers administered BRP through an injection into the muscle.

The results were striking. During the following hour, the treated animals consumed up to 50% less food than expected, suggesting that BRP could strongly influence hunger.

The scientists then examined whether repeated treatment could produce sustained changes in body weight. Obese mice received daily BRP injections for 14 days. By the end of the experiment, the treated mice had lost an average of 3 grams, while untreated control mice had gained approximately 3 grams.

Importantly, nearly all the weight lost by the BRP-treated mice came from body fat rather than muscle. Preserving muscle is an important goal in obesity treatment because muscle tissue supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.

The treated animals also showed improvements in glucose and insulin tolerance. These measurements reflect how effectively the body handles sugar and responds to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells.

Together, the findings suggest that BRP may influence both appetite and metabolic health, although it remains unknown whether people would experience comparable benefits.

Could BRP Avoid Common Ozempic Side Effects?

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery is the possibility that BRP could provide weight loss benefits while avoiding some unwanted effects associated with semaglutide and similar medications.

To investigate potential side effects, the researchers monitored the behavior and physical responses of the treated mice and pigs. They found no significant differences in movement, water consumption, anxiety-related behavior, or fecal output compared with control animals.

The absence of changes in fecal production was particularly interesting because constipation is a known side effect of medications such as Ozempic. The experiments also showed that BRP promoted fat loss without the substantial muscle loss that can accompany some weight reduction treatments.

Nausea is another common concern with existing GLP-1 medications, although animal experiments cannot fully establish whether BRP would prevent that symptom in people. Human testing will be essential to determine the molecule's actual side effect profile.

Additional investigations into brain activity and other physiological responses reinforced the idea that BRP works differently from semaglutide. The peptide activated distinct neuronal and metabolic pathways rather than simply copying the effects of GLP-1.

This difference may explain why the researchers observed strong appetite suppression without several of the behavioral and digestive changes they were monitoring.

What Comes Next for the Potential Ozempic Alternative?

Despite the encouraging findings, BRP is still at an early stage of development. Researchers need to understand more about exactly how the molecule communicates with cells and how its effects might be sustained over longer periods.

One priority is identifying the cell surface receptors that recognize BRP. Receptors are specialized proteins that respond to particular chemical signals, allowing cells to detect messages and trigger appropriate biological responses. Determining which receptors BRP activates could help explain its effects on hunger and metabolism.

The team also wants to investigate ways of extending the molecule's activity inside the body. Peptides can be broken down relatively quickly, potentially requiring frequent injections. A longer-lasting version of BRP could make treatment more convenient if it eventually proves effective in people.

The ultimate challenge will be establishing whether its apparent advantages in animals translate into meaningful benefits for patients. Clinical trials will need to evaluate its safety, effectiveness, appropriate dosage, and potential side effects before it could become a practical obesity treatment.

"The lack of effective drugs to treat obesity in humans has been a problem for decades," Svensson said. "Nothing we've tested before has compared to semaglutide's ability to decrease appetite and body weight. We are very eager to learn if it is safe and effective in humans."

Scientists from the University of California, Berkeley; the University of Minnesota; and the University of British Columbia also participated in the research.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01DK125260, P30DK116074, K99AR081618 and GM113854), the SPARK Translational Research Program at Stanford, Stanford Bio-X, the Stanford Maternal and Child Health Research Institute, the American Heart Association, a Stanford Medicine Dean's Fellowship Award, the Carlsberg Foundation, and the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance.

Svensson and Coassolo are named inventors on patents involving the use of BRP peptides to treat metabolic disorders. Svensson is also a cofounder of Merrifield Therapeutics.

#768. Ye Settles Lawsuit Over ‘Gun to My Head’ Sample From Descendant of Holocaust Survivors

German singer-songwriter Alice Merton claimed she had expressly denied the rapper's clearance request due to his history of antisemitism.

Ye (formerly Kanye West) has settled a lawsuit that accused him of sampling a song by German singer-songwriter Alice Merton even though she had rejected clearance due to the rapper’s history of antisemitism.

A Nov. 6 court filing, obtained by Billboard, stated that Ye and Merton have reached a settlement “conditioned on the parties’ completion of certain performance obligations.” Deal terms were not disclosed, and reps for both sides did not immediately return requests for comment.

Merton sued Ye last year, alleging his 2024 track “Gun to My Head” sampled her earlier song “Blindside” without permission. Merton said she had expressly denied Ye’s clearance request months earlier because, as a direct descendant of Holocaust survivors, she did not want to be associated with the rapper’s past antisemitic remarks.

Ye’s lawyers argued in response that Merton did not have the proper evidence for a copyright claim. They also pointed out that “Gun to My Head” has never been available on streaming; it was released on a digital deluxe version of Vultures 2, which was only available for purchase during a two-day period in 2024.

Merton’s case had been scheduled to go to trial this coming March. In October — a month before the settlement was reached — a judge denied Ye’s request to remove all references to the Holocaust and antisemitism from the lawsuit.

Ye has been sued more than a dozen times over the course of his career for allegedly using unlicensed samples and interpolations in his music. The rapper has settled many of these claims. He took one to trial for the first time earlier this year, and a jury ultimately held him liable for infringing an instrumental track on an early version of his chart-topping 2021 album Donda.

Meanwhile, Ye’s career has been mired in controversy around his antisemitism since 2022. He issued a lengthy apology in the Wall Street Journal this past January for years of public hate speech, including praise of Hitler and selling swastika T-shirts. Ye wrote in this apology, which preceded the release of his latest album Bully, that these controversial comments had stemmed from a 2002 car crash that caused severe brain damage and bipolar disorder.

“I regret and am deeply mortified by my actions in that state, and am committed to accountability, treatment and meaningful change,” Ye wrote. “It does not excuse what I did, though. I am not a Nazi or an antisemite. I love Jewish people.”

Ye has since worked to mount a comeback, playing to huge crowds at an ongoing run of stadium shows this year. But the rapper’s past is still haunting him, and shows in the U.K. and Poland have been canceled due to government concerns about his previous antisemitic statements. Senator Rick Scott (R-Fla.) also ran a public, though unsuccessful, campaign to stop Ye from performing at Tampa, Fla.’s Raymond James Stadium in June.

Editor's note for Nov. 13: Watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT) in the window above here.

SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.

Starship is scheduled to launch on its 15th test flight today from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). SpaceX plans to bring both of Starship's stages back to Starbase for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something it has never done before.

You can watch it all live here at Space.com. And there should be a lot to see: Starship Flight 15 will last more than 22 hours, if all goes according to plan.

Starship consists of two elements: a huge booster known as Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship, or Ship for short. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight.

The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said.

SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy, pulling the feat off on three previous Starship test flights. But it has never tried to do so with Ship, which flies farther and faster than the booster and is therefore a more challenging vehicle to recover.

So today's flight is a pretty big deal for SpaceX.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," the company wrote in a Flight 15 mission description.

The action will unspool over two days, if all goes to plan. Super Heavy will return to Starbase for a touchdown just 6.5 minutes after launch, but Ship will continue on to low Earth orbit.

The upper stage will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, during a 42-minute stretch beginning about 35 minutes after liftoff. This will be just the second batch of V3 spacecraft to reach orbit, after the 26 that went up on Flight 14 on Sept. 28.

Ship will then stay aloft for nearly a full day. The mission plan calls for the upper stage to return to Starbase for its chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), about 22.5 hours after liftoff.

There's no guarantee things will go according to plan, however. SpaceX will call off a Ship catch if the vehicle experiences any issues during Flight 15. If something crops up, the company will steer Ship to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, either near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

So it'll be a busy weekend for SpaceX, and for space fans who want to keep tabs on the mission. And we can help you out there, with our Flight 15 updates page.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. #765. MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures

Scientists have spent decades trying to control how tiny particles connect to form advanced materials. Now, researchers at MIT and their collaborators have discovered that doing the exact opposite of what was previously believed necessary can produce remarkable results.

Instead of relying on rigid molecular connections to hold nanoparticles in carefully planned arrangements, the team developed extremely flexible connectors that bend and adjust as particles come together. This unexpected strategy gives scientists a new way to control how nanoparticles organize themselves, allowing them to create crystal structures that have never been observed before.

The discovery could help overcome a major obstacle in materials science and open new possibilities for creating substances with precisely engineered properties. Potential applications include electronics, medicine, energy technologies, agriculture, and chemical manufacturing.

The findings, described in a paper that will appear in Nature Materials, demonstrate how the flexibility and electrical charges of molecular connectors can determine the structures that nanoparticles form.

MIT Researchers Challenge 20 Years of Materials Science

"People are interested in nanoparticle superlattices because of the promise of building designer materials where you have more say in what types of structures they can actually build into," says Rob Macfarlane, the Richard P. Simmons (1953) Professor in Metallurgy in MIT's Department of Materials Science and Engineering. "This is a new approach in nanoparticle assembly that hasn't been investigated before. It's exciting to have a new tool that is so counterintuitive. It's the exact opposite of what the dogma has been for 20 years: that you need to make connector ligands rigid, and any deviation causes assembly to fail. We showed if you just crank it all the way to the opposite extreme, it works just as well."

The research team also included MIT PhD candidate Nicholas Sbalbi, University of Delaware doctoral student Stephen Kronenberger, MIT undergraduate Hana Shinzawa, Matthew Ye PhD '26, and Arthi Jayaraman, a former professor at the University of Delaware.

At the heart of the discovery is a basic principle of materials science: The way a material's smallest components are arranged determines how that material behaves.

"That means if you know what your building blocks are and how they're arranged, you can explain what properties materials have," Macfarlane says. "Controlling that is how you make materials that have new properties."

This principle is especially important when working with nanoparticles, which are extremely small pieces of matter whose shapes, sizes, and properties can be adjusted for different purposes. Scientists already use individual nanoparticles in technologies involving drug delivery, energy storage, computing, and sensors.

But turning these tiny building blocks into larger, organized materials presents a difficult challenge.

Why Nanoparticles Are So Difficult to Control

One of the biggest obstacles is controlling how nanoparticles attach to one another. Scientists need to determine not only how many neighboring particles each nanoparticle connects with, but also the directions in which those connections form.

Without that control, nanoparticles tend to assemble into tightly packed arrangements that restrict the variety of structures researchers can produce. This limits their ability to create materials with unusual or specialized properties.

Researchers have traditionally approached the problem in two ways. One strategy involves changing the shapes of nanoparticles to influence how they fit together. Another involves modifying specific areas of their surfaces so that only certain regions attract neighboring particles.

In effect, scientists attempt to control where the particles stick to one another, much like designing puzzle pieces that can connect only in particular positions.

Although these methods can produce useful structures, they are often complicated, highly specialized, and difficult to adapt for large-scale production.

"The challenge with both of those approaches is they're difficult to do synthetically as we make the particles," Macfarlane explains. "The methods for defining stickiness that have been developed are always bespoke: They work for one material, at one size scale, in one condition. It's good for studying, but you can't do much with it."

Both strategies also depend on molecular connectors called ligands. These molecules attach to the surfaces of nanoparticles and help link neighboring particles together.

Traditionally, researchers have tried to make these ligands rigid so the connections remain at carefully controlled angles. This helps maintain a desired arrangement, but it also restricts the types of structures that can form and the functions they can perform.

The MIT team decided to explore a radically different possibility.

A Surprising Discovery About Flexible Molecular Bonds

Rather than forcing molecular connectors to remain in fixed positions, the researchers wondered whether giving them almost complete freedom to bend could offer an entirely new form of control.

"We thought, 'Let's do the exact opposite: make the bonds so flexible it doesn't matter what direction they're initially pointing.' The ligands can then reorganize as the particles come together, and that reorganization itself limits how many neighbors each particle can bind," Macfarlane says.

The idea reverses the usual approach to nanoparticle assembly. Instead of controlling the orientation of every connection in advance, the scientists allow the connectors to adjust naturally as the particles interact.

Macfarlane's laboratory has spent years developing ways to construct different types of nanoparticles using attached polymer chains. Polymers are large molecules made of repeating smaller units, and their flexibility makes them useful for creating adjustable molecular connections.

For the new system, the team equipped nanoparticles with highly flexible ligands that carry electrical charges at their ends. Some have positive charges, while others have negative charges.

Because opposite electrical charges attract, the connector molecules naturally bend toward partners with the opposite charge. This attraction helps the nanoparticles join together, while the flexibility of the connectors influences how many connections each particle can make.

"The idea is, instead of defining a specific direction the bonds are going to occur in with complicated synthesis methods, we just said, 'The bonds are going to be as flexible as they want to be, and they'll spontaneously go to whatever valency is going to maximize bond stability,'" Macfarlane says.

In this context, valency refers to the number of connections a nanoparticle forms with its neighbors. By allowing the connectors to move freely, the researchers found that the system could naturally settle into stable arrangements without requiring every connection to be designed beforehand.

Scientists Create Crystal Structures Never Seen Before

Experiments led by Sbalbi demonstrated that the researchers could adjust the connections between nanoparticles by changing two relatively straightforward characteristics: the sizes of the particles and the lengths of their flexible molecular chains.

These adjustments altered how the particles assembled, giving the team control over the number of neighboring particles each one could connect with.

Most importantly, the researchers used this method to produce previously unseen crystal structures.

Crystals are materials whose building blocks form organized, repeating patterns. In this case, the repeating arrangements are made from nanoparticles rather than individual atoms or small molecules. Such ordered nanoparticle networks are often called superlattices.

By reducing the number of connections between neighboring particles, the team was able to create more open arrangements instead of the densely packed structures that commonly form during nanoparticle assembly.

"Without having to predesign where the particles connect or what their shapes are, we can control the number of bonds each particle has," Macfarlane explains. "The amount of flexibility of the polymer dictates how many bonds it has. It allows us to lower the number of bonds each particle has and make lattices we have never seen before."

The results suggest that molecular flexibility, once viewed as an obstacle to precise nanoparticle assembly, can instead become a powerful tool for engineering new material structures.

A New Path Toward Customizable Designer Materials

The researchers believe their method could bring scientists closer to a long-sought goal in materials science: choosing the properties of individual nanoparticles independently of the larger structures into which they assemble.

Ideally, scientists could select nanoparticles for their electrical, optical, chemical, or other useful characteristics and then organize those particles into whatever arrangement best serves a particular application.

In practice, however, existing assembly methods have made that level of flexibility difficult to achieve.

"We in the nanoparticle assembly community talk about having completely independent control over what your particle is and what assembly it goes into," Macfarlane says. "In theory, that should be the case. In reality, it absolutely has not been."

The new approach could help close that gap. Because the researchers can influence nanoparticle arrangements through the flexibility of their connectors and the attraction between electrical charges, they may be able to create a wider variety of structures without the complicated manufacturing techniques required by traditional methods.

The team also sees the discovery as a promising route toward producing customizable materials at larger scales, potentially helping move nanoparticle technologies beyond laboratory experiments and into practical use.

Potential Applications in Electronics, Medicine, and Energy

The ability to build more open and varied nanoparticle structures could prove particularly valuable for developing advanced materials.

In photonics, which involves controlling and manipulating light, precisely organized nanoparticles could help researchers engineer materials with specialized optical properties. In chemical catalysis, where substances accelerate chemical reactions, new particle arrangements could create opportunities to improve the way catalysts operate.

The approach may also support future developments in medicine, agriculture, electronics, and energy technologies.

A major advantage is that nanoparticles can already possess a wide range of desirable properties. By controlling how those particles come together, scientists may be able to combine their individual capabilities in new ways.

"Nanoparticle superlattices offer a way to create designer materials where your building blocks have all sort sorts of unique properties," Macfarlane says. "But just densely packing these nanoparticles together limits your applications. This offers a way to get less dense formations of nanoparticles, and that's where a lot of the interesting applications are."

Although further development will be needed to translate the method into commercial technologies, the discovery establishes molecular flexibility as a new strategy for creating materials with tailored structures.

Instead of treating bending molecular connections as a problem to eliminate, scientists may now be able to use that flexibility to unlock arrangements that rigid designs could not easily achieve.

The research received partial support from the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the U.S. Army, and the U.S. Navy.

Cara Delevingne knows the holiday season can be tricky for single people, so she shared tips and tricks to avoid the holiday slump in an exclusive interview with E! News at GQ’s Men of the Year event.

Cara Delevingne is strutting into the holiday season with a game plan.

As Thanksgiving and Christmas fast approach, the British supermodel admitted this time of year “can be tricky,” especially for those who might be entering the holiday season single.

“It can bring around a lot of like, ‘Oh, my gosh, am I in a relationship? Is that lonely? Presents are expensive,’” Delevingne told E! News’ Will Marfuggi in an exclusive interview at GQ’s Men of the Year event Nov. 12. “They can bring up a lot.”

Despite the holiday hubbub, though, the 34-year-old—who has been dating girlfriend Minke since 2022—emphasized ‘tis the season for rest and relaxation since we all “work too hard.” And that goes for everyone—despite relationship status.

“It's a time to have off, even if you're single, even if you're alone on the holiday,” she continued. “Find friends. Have Friendsgiving. Just find people. If not, catch up on the movies, watch TV shows.”

After all, a little R&R is how Delevingne has been leaning into the holiday season as of late. When the holidays kicked off not long after she began her sobriety journey in September 2022, she and Minke (real name Leah Mason) kept it chill that Christmas and New Year’s in Utah.

“It was just the two of us,” she told Vogue in March 2023. “I was in bed by 12:15 a.m. on New Year’s Eve having the nicest time.”

And since reconnecting with Minke in 2021—the pair had lost touch after attending grade school together in their teens—the Suicide Squad actress has found that she wouldn’t want anyone else by her side as she navigates her sobriety.

“These past two years have been A LOT of life. I spent so long looking for my partner in crime, little did I know that it would be someone I went to school with (and had a baby gay crush on).”

#762. Viva La Lisa! 5 Best Moments From LISA’s Opening Night in Las Vegas

The BLACKPINK superstar made history at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace with seven live debuts & an unreleased song.

Las Vegas has new residency royalty: queen LISA.

The BLACKPINK rapper, singer and dancer became the first K-pop artist to headline a Las Vegas residency Thursday night (Nov. 12), opening her six-show “Viva La Lisa” engagement at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace with a fast-paced, 90-minute production, high-energy choreography and enough costume changes to fill a showgirl’s dressing room.

The Thai-born superstar, who made her solo Coachella debut in 2025 and appeared in season 3 of HBO’s The White Lotus, has plenty of material to work with. Her debut solo album, Alter Ego, arrived in February 2025, followed by the six-track EP Press Play on Oct. 23. She performed the entire EP — including several live debuts — along with established solo hits, collaborations, and one previously unreleased song.

Each chapter of “Viva” presented a facet of LISA’s stage persona, from a crimson-clad goddess emerging from a lotus blossom to a futuristic provocateur, a playful pop star and a dark angel. Using a multi-level stage, aerial apparatuses, and a hydraulic satellite stage, LISA met her fans where they were — sometimes even at eye level — while the production moved between cinematic fantasy, club culture, and Thai imagery.

Here are five of the best moments from opening night.

For the opening sequence, the pop culture icon was lifted from the stage in an aerial hoop in an explosion of crimson feathers and cascading tulle, framed by an enormous golden lotus that appeared to blossom around her.

During “Tarantino,” the opening track from Press Play, the stage became a showgirl’s dressing room, complete with clothing racks, mirrors and sparkling costumes. Dancers attended to Lisa as she shed her feathered entrance piece and slipped into a red coat. The audience was invited behind the curtain, where the business of becoming a showgirl was every bit as theatrical as the performance itself.

Then came “FXCK UP THE WORLD,” and the fantasy took a sharp turn toward The Matrix. Green digital graphics illuminated an industrial maze of platforms and scaffolding as Lisa continued shedding layers, revealing a red-lace bodysuit and thigh-high black boots.

For the live debut of “V12,” she pulled on an oversized burgundy fur-style coat and strutted through a metropolitan streetscape as flames rose behind her. By “Rockstar,” the chapter’s closing number, she commanded an elevated platform as dancers moved around and beneath her. Three songs made their live debuts in the opening chapter: “Tarantino,” “V12” and “BADGRRRL.”

After the opening chapter’s succession of dramatic costume reveals, Lisa turned up the temperature with “Sweat,” another live debut from Press Play, nailing a sultry dance sequence with her male troupe.

The mood became more playful for “Elastigirl,” whose intro incorporated elements of Britney Spears’ “Gimme More.” Lisa took command of an elevated platform in towering black boots, with strips of gray fabric swinging from her hips that emphasized her incredible moves.

The chapter also featured “Goals,” her collaboration with Anitta and Rema, and “Rapunzel,” which gave Lisa a welcome opportunity to address the audience directly. Moving to the front of the stage, she crouched down to get closer to fans and shared that it was one of her “favorite songs.”

The chapter closed with “Money,” her breakout solo hit from 2021, followed by an extended dance-break remix incorporating Rihanna’s “Bitch Better Have My Money” and BLACKPINK’s “JUMP.” A lucky few in the pit were able to collect some of the “Lisa bucks” as she made it rain with her own currency.

For all the pyrotechnics, aerial action and monumental production, some of the evening’s most memorable moments came when Lisa brought the performance down to a more personal level.

In the third chapter, she became the good angel and shifted the mood with “Moonlit Floor,” followed by “Dream,” performed on a hydraulic B-stage in the audience that rises to the balconies of The Colosseum. During “When I’m With You,” she ventured into the crowd to greet fans. The chapter concluded with “Born Again,” her collaboration with Doja Cat and RAYE.

“Cut U Off” and “Cobra,” both from press play, made their live debuts in the fourth chapter, bringing the number of songs performed from the new EP to six. Released just three weeks ago, the project provides the musical framework for much of “Viva La Lisa.”

“New Woman,” her collaboration with Rosalía, came before Lisa introduced “Leave With Me,” an unreleased track.  At Las Vegas residencies, audiences often expect the greatest hits, but the amount of new material departed from the traditional formula. Lisa used the stage to reveal another side of her sound.

Lisa saved some of her most dramatic transformations for the final chapter, beginning with “Thunder” as storm clouds rolled across the towering video screens. For “Bad Angel,” her collaboration with electronic music producer Anyma, she emerged in a black costume with sculptural, winglike shoulders and thigh-high boots, looking every bit the fallen angel. The ominous imagery and dark theatricality gave the production a decidedly different atmosphere from the bright red costumes and playful choreography of the earlier chapters.

The mood shifted again for “SaWaDiKa,” the finale from Press Play, which brought Lisa’s Thai heritage to the forefront. The title is a stylized version of sawasdee kha, the traditional Thai greeting used to say hello or goodbye. Its Bangkok-filmed music video incorporates Muay Thai boxing, tuk-tuks and other references to Thai culture, presenting the sights and sounds of her homeland.

Lisa opened with “Tarantino” and finished with “SaWaDiKa,” bookending the five-chapter production with songs from Press Play. For an artist who has increasingly incorporated her Thai roots into her solo music, ending her first Las Vegas residency performance with a nod to where she came from felt particularly fitting.

And for Las Vegas, which has welcomed generations of pop royalty to its stages, the arrival of its first K-pop residency headliner marked the beginning of a fresh chapter.

#761. A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies

Astronomers have discovered an extraordinary ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, offering a possible preview of what could happen to our own Solar System billions of years from now. Even more surprising, the debris is divided into two distinct rings, with a clear gap between them that may be maintained by planetary bodies that somehow survived their star's death.

The discovery was made using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT). Unlike previously observed debris systems around dead stars, this one appears to contain two separate discs of material left behind by destroyed planets. Researchers believe two surviving objects may be shaping the unusual structure, including one potentially as large as Pluto or even the Moon.

"We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals," says Nicola Gentile Fusillo, an astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste in Italy and lead author of the study published in Nature Astronomy.

A Dead Star Surrounded by Planetary Wreckage

At the center of the system is J1328−1450, a white dwarf. These extremely dense stellar remnants form when stars similar to our Sun exhaust their fuel and reach the final stages of their evolution. After expanding dramatically and shedding their outer layers, they leave behind their exposed cores.

This transformation can be catastrophic for nearby planets. As a star swells, it may engulf and destroy worlds orbiting too close to it. More distant rocky objects can survive the initial upheaval, although gravitational disturbances may eventually tear some of them apart. Their remains can form rotating discs of debris around the dead star.

Astronomers have observed such debris discs around other white dwarfs, but J1328−1450 is different. Instead of a single ring of vaporized planetary material, it has two concentric rings, meaning one lies farther from the star than the other. The rings remain clearly separated, creating an unusual structure that scientists are now trying to explain.

"The structure we see in this system is particularly intriguing because the two gaseous rings are remarkably stable and remain separated by a gap," says co-author Felipe Lagos-Vilches, an astronomer at the University of Warwick, UK, and at the Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile.

"The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized," adds Gentile Fusillo, who is also affiliated with the INAF-Astronomical Observatory of Trieste.

Two Surviving Worlds May Be Shaping the Rings

The researchers suspect that two surviving planetary bodies, each traveling along a separate orbit, are responsible for maintaining the double ring structure.

One of these objects, associated with the inner ring, is thought to be comparable in size to a typical asteroid, measuring only a few kilometers across. The other, farther from the star, could be much larger, potentially reaching the size of Pluto or even our Moon.

Such objects are known as planetesimals, a term used for smaller solid bodies associated with the formation and evolution of planetary systems. Although the two suspected survivors have not been directly observed, their gravitational influence could help explain why the debris remains organized into two distinct rings rather than forming one continuous disc.

The evidence comes from observations collected with the X-Shooter instrument on ESO's VLT in Chile's Atacama Desert. The instrument analyzes light across a broad range of wavelengths, allowing astronomers to examine the chemical makeup and motion of material surrounding distant objects.

Previously discovered debris discs around white dwarfs have shared a recognizable observational signature consistent with a single, flat, rotating disc. J1328−1450 breaks that pattern. Its observations instead reveal the unique fingerprint of a double disc, providing evidence of a far more complicated arrangement of planetary remains.

Chemical Clues Reveal the Remains of Destroyed Planets

The debris also contains important clues about the worlds that once orbited the star.

Astronomers detected calcium, oxygen, magnesium, and iron, elements commonly found in rocky planetary material throughout our Solar System. Their presence indicates that the rings contain remnants of solid bodies rather than simply gas left over from the star itself.

More intriguingly, the two rings have noticeably different chemical compositions. The inner ring contains substantial amounts of magnesium gas, while the outer ring is largely depleted of magnesium.

This difference suggests that the material in the two rings may have originated from separate planets with different compositions. If so, the system could preserve evidence of multiple destroyed worlds.

Another possibility is that both rings contain material from different layers of the same planetary body. For example, one ring could contain debris from a planet's outer crust, while the other contains material from deeper inside, such as its core.

Either explanation would offer valuable insight into the destruction of rocky worlds and the complex processes that can continue long after a star has exhausted its fuel.

A Possible Preview of Our Solar System's Future

The discovery also raises a compelling question about the ultimate fate of our own planetary neighborhood.

Billions of years from now, the Sun will undergo a similar transformation. It will expand into a red giant, shed its outer layers, and eventually become a white dwarf. During this process, the inner Solar System will experience enormous changes, and Earth itself may be destroyed.

Yet the observations of J1328−1450 suggest that the death of a star does not necessarily mean the complete disappearance of its planetary system. Some objects may survive, while others could be shattered into debris that continues orbiting the stellar remnant in complex arrangements.

By studying this distant dead star and its unusual double rings, astronomers are gaining a rare opportunity to investigate what remains after a planetary system experiences such a violent transformation.

"The system therefore offers a remarkable glimpse of what the future of planetary systems, including systems like our own, might look like," concludes Lagos-Vilches.

Materials provided by European Southern Observatory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#760. Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS.
