#687. JB Smoove Talks Creativity and Fighting AI Fears, Evan Shapiro Breaks Down the Digital Entertainment Economy at Variety’s Business Managers Breakfast

Candice Bergen presents the Business Manager of the Year kudo to Citrin Cooperman's Arnie Herrmann

JB Smoove brought his signature creative swagger and Evan Shapiro broke down the digital entertainment economy during lively conversations held as part of Variety‘s annual Business Managers Breakfast presented by City National Bank.

The event, held Thursday in West Hollywood, hosted Variety’s 2026 Business Managers Elite honorees and recognized Citrin Cooperman’s Arnie Herrmann as Business Manager of the Year. Attendees listened to a keynote conversation with actor, comedian, producer and writer Smoove, as well as a presentation from media analyst Evan Shapiro. Related Stories Aero Films Acquires North American Rights to Ivy League Satire 'Kingston' (EXCLUSIVE)

Read below for key takeaways from the breakfast:

City National Bank president and CEO Howard Hammond kicked off the morning.

“You’re a core part of the past of City National Bank,” he told the SRO crowd of business managers. “But more importantly, our future will always be intertwined with entertainment and sports.”

He thanked attendees for their support as clients and “blunt feedback,” and recalled a conversation where Arnie Herrmann said the two things that made his career what it is today were trust and service.

The actor, comedian and entrepreneur sat down with Variety executive editor for television Michael Schneider, where he emphasized the importance of taking control.

“I do believe you have to start early and think about where you’re going to end up at. But be open to changing yourself as you go along,” Smoove said. If you don’t, “you are basically in a mental zombie apocalypse” trying to catch up when you finally get hungry for success.

Smoove said he himself has been at least five different people in his lifetime, and credits his comedic senses and thick skin for that flexibility and resilience. “Everything I ever wanted to do, I’m taking a swing in,” he said.

Still, he doesn’t limit himself to only being a comedian. Smoove was a finalist to join the cast of “Saturday Night Live,” but was eventually hired as a writer. It wasn’t something he had done before, but “sometimes you gotta play the long ball for later,” he said. “You prepare for that moment, and I’m great in the moment.”

LISTEN to highlights from the JB Smoove and Evan Shapiro conversations on Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast

The comedian tells people all the time to take an improv class. “You’ll be surprised how that’s going to come in handy when you’re selling real estate, or you’re building a company or you’re a small business owner,” Smoove said. “It helps being able to change gears in the moment.”

Smoove launched comedy-focused creative advertising agency The First Darrin in 2025 with United Entertainment Group CEO Jarrod Moses. With that company, he focuses on creating memorable and daring campaigns.

He also formed Alternate Side Productions and has several projects in the works under that banner. “You got to almost constantly sell yourself, and there’s nothing wrong with that,” Smoove said. “I think I’m a great salesman, and when I show up, it’s always 200%.”

Smoove credits his successes — like appearing on “Curb Your Enthusiasm” or in two Spider-Man films — to, again, driving his own vehicle. “You gotta make chess moves,” he said.

With his production company and ad agency, Smoove shows his creativity. “If you’re scared of AI, you ain’t shit,” he said. “If you are worried about something that’s coming in, you don’t have faith in the human mind.”

Evan Shapiro spoke with Cynthia Littleton, Variety co-Editor in Chief, about his take on the “affinity economy” and its impact on the entertainment industry.

Shapiro calls it the affinity economy, rather than the attention economy. He sees the companies that are successful have a creator mindset and serve the entire consumer.

“Most content does want to be free,” Shapiro said. His research shows that YouTube is at the top for total attention, which he credits to the fact that is free.

Ultimately, though, any major business will be “detrimental” to artists. “It’s not a corporation,” Shapiro said. “It’s not a foundation. It’s not a museum. It’s not a charity. They’re in it to make money.”

One of 2026’s biggest box office successes came in the form of “Obsession,” from YouTuber Curry Barker. “This guy is the new Tarantino,” Shapiro said. “It’s not because he has a massive following. It’s because he knows how to engage fans today.”

The quality of fan engagement and ability to manage that community is essential for artists today. “There’s a reason why The Rock can’t open a movie on his own without Kevin Hart,” Shapiro pointed out.

The box office may seem like it has recovered, Shapiro said, but that is because the ticket price has increased 128% this century. Will there ever be “Seinfeld” and “Friends” level syndication profits flowing in again to creatives and others in Hollywood’s creative community? Shapiro thinks so, but it will be with a different approach. “Hollywood and the traditional media ecosystem are not being disrupted,” he said. “They’re being reinvented.”

Emmy and Golden Globe Award-winning actress Candice Bergen introduced Arnie Herrmann, following two video messages from two other longtime Herrmann clients, Liam Neeson and Martin Scorsese.

“He’s intelligent, he’s modest, he has a nobility, he behaves himself,” Bergen said of Herrmann. “He’s just someone that you really would appreciate as a friend and as a guy to handle your cash.”

Longtime business manager Arnie Herrmann spoke from the heart as he accepted Variety‘s Business Manager of the Year kudo. Based in New York, Herrmann has nearly 40 of experience as a business manager and joined his current firm of Citrin Cooperman in 2010.

He recalled a colleague asking him during a brief stint at a large accounting firm, “Why keep score if we can play the game?” Herrmann took that advice to heard and left that firm to work for a boutique outfit, where he discovered his love for the business management profession.

Herrmann highlighted how lucky he feels to advise legendary entertainers, trailblazing women journalists, EGOT-winning producers, Michelin Award-winning chefs, music executives and New York City real estate pioneers. He shared a message he received from a longtime (unnamed) client when he told the client that he was nearing retirement.

“You’ve served your firm and your clients so spectacularly with such heart. Now it’s Act Three, the most important, the last one, the one where you’re meant to put everything you’ve learned in Acts One and Two and put it to work so that it’s the richest and most satisfying of all,” Herrmann read from the message. “I never like goodbyes, but it’s not. It’s farewell, and Arnie, if someone deserves farewell, it’s you. So I just wanted to say this again in a form where my voice can’t catch, because you sit up way high in our lives and liability be damned, you are much more to me than a business manager and you have been for so long.”

Herrmann also thanked his longtime clients, Variety, Citrin Cooperman colleagues, City National Bank and his family.

“The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl famously once said, ‘He who has a why can bear almost any how,’” Herrmann said. “Now he said this under dire circumstances, but in a much lighter scenario, I can apply it here. If the ‘how’ are the long hours, the missed family time, the missed events, the ‘why’ is my love for you, my family.”

#685. Number of international students arriving in US plunges — worrying scientists

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

International students earn almost 40% of science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.Credit: Bill Pugliano/Getty

The number of international students arriving in the United States in August for the start of the academic year has fallen by 28% since 2024, reaching the lowest level since the depths reached in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Data from the federal National Travel and Tourism Office show that the number of incoming student-visa holders fell from 387,000 in August 2024 to 277,000 in August 2026 (see ‘Students stay away’). The trend has been driven by a decline in students from India and China, whose numbers dropped by about 50,000 and 23,000, respectively, from 2024 to 2026.

Source: National Travel and Tourism Office (NTTO); Nature analysis.

The number of applications from international students to US PhD programmes also declined over the past year, falling 21% from 2025 to 2026, according to a survey of 55 members of the Association of American Universities (AAU), a coalition of research-intensive schools.

These decreases are squeezing already strained university budgets, and researchers worry about the impact on US science. “I can’t imagine a more effective way for the US to cede its dominance in critical scientific fields to China and Europe than by reducing international students,” says Nigel Goldenfeld, a physicist at the University of California, San Diego. In 2024, international students earned 38% of the science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing

The administration of US president Donald Trump has introduced several restrictions on visas and international travel since Trump took office in early 2025. Last month, the administration also attempted to place a US$100,000 levy on science and engineering students enrolling in extended Optional Practical Training (OPT), a work programme used by hundreds of thousands of recent graduates that is the largest pipeline of scientific talent into the United States. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which issued the proposal, stated that it is meant to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers”.

Federal judges have suspended the OPT charge and other efforts that the administration made to curb immigration. But higher-education specialists link these attempts to the large decrease in new overseas students, who, they say, can no longer count a US education as a stable investment. “Uncertainty has become policy, and that has registered in the hearts and minds of students,” says Chris Glass, a higher-education researcher at Boston College in Massachusetts.

The United Kingdom, Canada and Australia have also seen drops in enrolment of international students after placing new limits on these populations. But the US policies are especially restrictive, Glass says.

A spokesperson for the White House did not respond to Nature’s request for comment.

#684. Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon

Far below the ocean's surface, a constant snowfall drifts through the darkness. But unlike the frozen flakes that fall from the sky, this underwater snow consists of tiny clumps of waste, dead organisms, and other debris. Known as marine snow, these particles contain everything from mucus and animal feces to silt and the remains of microscopic plankton.

As this material sinks, it carries enormous quantities of carbon from the upper ocean toward the seafloor. Researchers estimate that marine snow removes more than 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters each year. Yet only about two gigatons reach depths where that carbon can remain stored for hundreds or even thousands of years.

Why so much carbon fails to make it into the deep ocean has long puzzled scientists. Now, researchers from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have identified a surprisingly important factor: how sticky the marine snow is.

Their findings, published October 8 in the journal Science, show that the viscosity, or thickness and gooeyness, of marine snow influences how quickly bacteria break it apart and how far it can sink. According to the researchers, the stickiest particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as particles with a thinner, less viscous consistency.

Marine snow plays an important role in Earth's carbon cycle, the natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms. By transporting carbon into deep water, sinking particles can keep some of it isolated from the atmosphere for centuries or longer.

However, not every particle survives the journey. Bacteria feed on marine snow as it descends, gradually breaking down the material and affecting how much carbon reaches the ocean's depths.

The new research provides the first detailed look at how living bacteria interact with the physical structure of marine snow and, more broadly, mucus itself. These interactions are important well beyond the ocean's carbon cycle. Similar relationships between bacteria and mucus help sustain coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive systems of humans and other animals.

Until recently, scientists lacked the technology to observe these interactions at the microscopic scale needed to understand them.

A Four-Year Quest to See Inside Marine Snow

The project began in 2021, when Bryce Inman, then a postdoctoral researcher at Scripps Oceanography, set out to explore what he calls "the muscoscape."

"Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible," said Inman.

Together with colleagues including Farooq Azam, a microbiologist and professor emeritus at Scripps, Inman spent four years trying to overcome that limitation. Multiple attempts were unsuccessful before the team finally developed a working technique in 2025.

Their solution combined 3D confocal microscopy with specially designed fluorescent molecules. Confocal microscopy uses light to capture detailed images at different depths within a sample, allowing researchers to reconstruct its structure in three dimensions. The fluorescent molecules helped make features of the material visible.

For the first time, the scientists could examine the "physical terrain" of individual marine snow particles while watching how living bacteria moved through and interacted with them.

The images revealed a surprisingly intricate microscopic environment, complete with structural differences that affect where bacteria can settle and how easily they can reach the material inside.

Much like snowflakes in the atmosphere, marine snow particles vary considerably. Each contains its own mixture of organic and inorganic materials, creating differences in composition, structure, and viscosity.

The researchers' new imaging approach, described in a companion study published in Nature Communications, revealed that bacteria preferentially colonize areas near a particle's surface where the material is less viscous.

The denser, stickier regions deeper inside are much harder for bacteria to penetrate.

"Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down," said Inman. "Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through"

This difference has important consequences for how long marine snow remains intact.

In laboratory experiments, the scientists observed that particles with greater viscosity resisted bacterial degradation and fragmentation for longer periods. Computer simulations further suggested that these stickier particles can descend to greater depths before breaking apart.

Based on these results, the team estimates that highly viscous marine snow can deliver more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.

The findings help explain why some sinking material transports carbon much farther into the ocean than other particles, even though both begin their journeys near the surface.

"How far marine snow can sink is a surprisingly complicated problem, and we have added another - very gooey - piece to the puzzle," said Inman.

A Discovery With Implications Beyond the Ocean

Although the research focuses on marine snow, its implications extend to many environments where bacteria interact with mucus.

Mucus is often regarded as a relatively simple, slippery substance. But the new imaging technology reveals that it has a complex internal landscape, with microscopic structures that can influence how bacteria behave.

Understanding these physical features could help scientists investigate biological processes in settings ranging from human digestive health to the recovery of damaged coral reefs.

The method also opens opportunities to explore interactions that previously could not be observed directly, providing researchers with a new way to study the microscopic environments inhabited by bacteria.

Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, "has a surprising amount of structure," Inman said. "There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we're really examining this physical habitat."

The discovery adds an important missing piece to scientists' understanding of how carbon travels through the ocean. It also demonstrates that something as seemingly ordinary as the thickness of underwater slime can have far-reaching consequences for the planet's natural systems.

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Simons Foundation and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.

#683. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO: Successor, reactions, live updates

Jensen Huang officially resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday morning, a seismic event in the tech industry.

Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, with a nearly $4 trillion valuation, and Huang was the company's original CEO and co-founder. The company's board of directors shared a CEO transition plan on its website, saying Huang has also resigned as president and as a member of the board, effective immediately.

The company's CFO, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO, while also maintaining her CFO responsibilities. The board has begun searching for a new CEO, looking both inside and outside the company.

The tech industry has been closely watching Nvidia and its stock ever since news first broke by the New York Times that Huang had not one, but two affairs, including one with an accused Chinese spy. Nvidia chips provide much of the compute that powers the fast-growing AI industry, and so Huang's alleged entanglement with a possible Chinese spy wasn't just a typical executive PR scandal, but a national security issue.

The story is still developing, so keep checking back at Mashable for the latest Nvidia news and live updates.

Last Friday, New York Times and Financial Times reported dropped a bomb on the tech industry. The publications reported that Huang had an affair with a woman the U.S. intelligence community believed to be a Chinese spy. China disputed these accusations, of course, but the Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio personally wrote a memo alerting President Donald Trump to the situation in the spring.

On Nov. 8, Huang posted a personal message to the Nvidia website, admitting to and apologizing for the affair.

"I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

It was unclear whether Huang would be able to hold on to his position as CEO, and the Nvidia board of directors announced it had opened an investigation into the incident.

But on Wednesday, news of a second affair may have sealed Huang's fate. The New York Times reported that Huang had another extramarital affair with another Nvidia executive who reported to him. The Times identified that executive as Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.

This is a developing story. The latest Nvidia news will be posted live on this page...

#682. Seth Rogen on ‘The Invite,’ ‘Tangles,’ ‘The Studio’ Season 2, Reviving ‘Darkwing Duck’ and Why ‘Any A–hole Can Write That Joke’ Was the Best Advice He Ever Got

Awards Circuit Podcast: The roundtable discusses the 'I Play Rocky' screenplay debate and the new Disney movie 'Hexed'

For years, people have told me that Seth Rogen and I are voice twins.

Sitting across from him at the Middleburg Film Festival, deep in Virginia horse country, even Jeremy, the person recording our conversation, can confirm that the resemblance is very close. Even so, the year Rogen is having belongs entirely to him.

Coming off the historic Emmy run of “The Studio,” Rogen could have gone anywhere next. He chose to travel into the world of darkly comic relationship drama “The Invite” and the 2D animated world of Alzheimer’s disease with “Tangles,” a one-two punch nobody could have seen coming. Related Stories Aero Films Acquires North American Rights to Ivy League Satire 'Kingston' (EXCLUSIVE)

In “The Invite,” Olivia Wilde’s A24 dinner-party indie, Rogen plays Joe, a husband whose fraying marriage gets stress-tested over one excruciating evening with the upstairs neighbors, played by Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton. I think it’s his finest hour as an actor. On paper, it sounds like a “another Seth Rogen” role. On screen, he plays it in a way we didn’t expect and he credits Wilde for taking his and Norton’s ideas to heart.

“She could have just not used any of it,” he says. “and I just would not have been as funny in it.”

On the episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, Rogen discusses his one-two punch of “The Invite” and “Tangles,” along with the recently announced “Darkwing Duck” revival at Disney+, the awards-season satire threaded through Season 2 of “The Studio” and how “Steve Jobs” opened a door to a part of the industry he had never been invited into. Listen below!

Among comedians, he says, going dramatic “almost feels like a bit of a cheat code” and he recalls Jonah Hill predicting “Moneyball” (2011) would bring him the most acclaim of his career for doing the least (Hill was right, getting his first Oscar nom for supporting actor).

“Tangles,” on the other hand, is a different kind of gamble. The hand-drawn, black-and-white animated feature, adapted from Sarah Leavitt’s graphic memoir about her mother’s Alzheimer’s and directed by first-time feature filmmaker Leah Nelson, comes from Rogen’s Point Grey Pictures and features his voice alongside Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Abbi Jacobson, Bryan Cranston and Samira Wiley. In a category ruled by studio franchises, it is the outlier and it took 10 years to make and the Canadian multihyphenate always had his eye on what’s most important. “When we give up on it is when it doesn’t happen,” he says.

Independent Film Company and Sapan Studio open “Tangles” in theaters this year for an awards-qualifying run, with a wider expansion in early 2027. “The Invite” is streaming on HBO Max.

The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

You’re having quite a year, with two very different movies in “The Invite” and “Tangles.” You’re coming off “The Studio,” and there’s been a lot of anticipation about what you’ll do next. This is quite a one-two punch. How does this moment in your career feel?

I feel very lucky. You only want to hope that you’re learning more in life, that you’re getting better at making choices and that once you’ve decided to do something, you get better at being the best part of the team you can be. It’s incredibly nice and gratifying that, over the last few years, I feel like I’ve been doing work I’m very proud of and pushing myself to do things that are hopefully different from what I’ve done in the past. But I also feel very lucky to have people who have wanted to work with me and have been willing to. And part of it is coincidence. We’ve worked on “Tangles” for 10 years. We didn’t know it was going to come out now. Luck has a lot to do with these things coming to life in a way that makes it seem like I planned it.

Starting with “The Invite,” this might be your finest hour as an actor. On paper, it sounds like a movie Seth Rogen would make. Playing Joe, did you feel you were doing something you hadn’t done before? Did you have one of those out-of-body experiences?

As we were making the movie, I felt like I was being given the opportunity, at least in a movie, to do something that was very representative of my exact comedic, tonal and dramatic taste. What was really amazing about what Olivia did was that she allowed us to affect the tone of the film with our performances. She allowed me to insert humor in moments where it wasn’t originally going to be, which changes the tone of the whole thing. She allowed Edward to give dramatic monologues in places where they weren’t originally going to be. And then she allowed me to make jokes that subverted those moments in ways that weren’t originally scripted.

To me, that was an incredibly new and gratifying feeling. We weren’t just being invited to change the dialogue or our characters throughout the performing process. Olivia was allowing us to change the tone of the film itself with our performances. You could see it happening in real time. You could see that a scene was much funnier than we thought it would be. Or we thought a scene was going to be funny, but it was actually much more intense than we all thought. We were encouraged to play with that and not be too beholden to what it was originally conceived as, but instead feel it out as we were doing it.

I have to give her credit for using my stuff in a way that turned out very well. I throw a lot of stuff out there, and she could have edited this movie in a way that left out some of what I think are the funniest moments I generated as we were making it. The film probably still would have been very good, but I just wouldn’t have been as funny in it.

So I’m very proud that it’s a performance people seem to like, and I genuinely feel it’s one of my funnier performances. I’ve done dramatic work in the past, and I think among comedians it almost feels like a bit of a cheat code. If I’m not funny, everyone leans in a little bit more. I remember Jonah Hill was making “Moneyball,” and he said, “This is going to be the thing that I get the most acclaim for. And it’s for sure the easiest thing I’ve done, because I’m just doing less than I normally do.” And I’ve done things like that. So what’s nice is that I do feel like I was creating comedy throughout this film, and people are appreciating that. It isn’t just because it’s not funny that people are appreciating it, which is something I think a lot of comedians have experienced.

It’s the Jim Carrey cheat code. He gets to do “The Truman Show” and “Eternal Sunshine,” and suddenly we’re all saying, “My God.”

Yes. There was a time when comedians really pursued that and wanted that, and I think it was a very deliberate thing comedians were doing for a while. I totally get it. It’s totally legitimate. It’s just that, to me, I’m very proud of my ability to generate comedy on camera. I’ve always been most proud of my funny work. It’s obviously an honor to get to be in Steven Spielberg movies and things like that are certainly less comedic, and the fact that those filmmakers think I can serve their work in any way is very flattering. But I’m always thinking, if I could also bring my full ability to make this comedic, that would be great. That’s exactly what Olivia really encouraged me to do. So it was very gratifying to be able to bring that.

I love that comedic actors can make that transition so seamlessly. I’m also dying for directors who are known for drama to go the other way. I want to see the Christopher Nolan version of “Superbad.” I want them to take a swing like that.

Apparently, “Digger” is that. I haven’t seen it yet. It’s harder than it looks sometimes. It does go both ways. Comedians try to do drama, and sometimes it’s ill-fitting. Dramatic actors try to do comedy, and sometimes that’s ill-fitting, too. I’m not saying that film is that. I haven’t seen it. But it’s something I’ve seen happen.

Then there’s “Tangles,” which is about as far from “The Invite” as you can get. The animated feature category at the Oscars has been dominated by studio franchises for years, and now we have this hand-drawn, black-and-white film about Alzheimer’s. I think people need to hear the answer to this: How difficult is it to make a movie like this?

Really hard [laughs]. We’ve been working on it for 10 years, and I think maybe the last three years of that were production. So it was about seven years of us internally developing it, but also trying to find financing, putting together a cast that would be appealing to financiers, doing readings and making sure the script was really, really good.

And the movie itself was made incredibly differently. Most animated movies, these big studio ones, are made, then made again, then made again. You screen them, redo the third act, screen them again and redo the first act. This movie couldn’t be made that way. It had to be written and then executed, and we could change almost nothing. It’s hand-drawn, so the process of changing things, should you want to, is incredibly labor-intensive and arduous.

People like Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Bryan Cranston, Samira Wiley and Abbi Jacobson, along with so many of the amazing cast members, were honestly really helpful in getting the movie made. So was having a good script and filmmakers who, when those actors got in the room with them, were willing to let them take ownership of the material. It’s so gratifying that the movie even exists. We’ve spent so long working on it.

During those first seven years, how many times did you think, “This isn’t happening?”

I thought it would happen. So many things take a long time to get made. I truly believe that if we give up on it, that’s when it doesn’t happen. Sometimes we don’t give up, and we will bring it into existence through sheer brute force. This felt worth it because it was good. If something is good, I believe you can find a way to make it. “Superbad” took so long to get made. And then there were things like “Pineapple Express” and “Sausage Party,” all these movies we worked on for so long before they were made. To me, 10 years is normal.

“Darkwing Duck” because I’m a child of the ’80s and ’90s. Congratulations on the Emmy for “The Muppet Show,” and obviously we have “The Studio” Season 2 coming. But nothing excites me more than this cartoon classic that Mark Hamill has a role in! Did that casting fall into your lap?

The cast is really great. We just cast a Scrooge McDuck who might be the most exciting casting I could ever imagine. I’ll tell you after. But it’s incredible. We’ve been working on it for a very long time. You get caught up in these corporate restructurings, but we’ve been working on “Darkwing Duck” for years and years. I’ve been watching the episodes, and they’re amazing. They’re coming together so well, and the animation is beautiful and really inventive.

I was actually surprised you didn’t go the movie route.

I’m glad we didn’t. The TV nature of it was very appealing to us, honestly. As nice as it is to make a hand-drawn, black-and-white animated film, it’s also nice to extract every penny Disney’s willing to put into a thing. Getting to work in both those ways is nice. But with something like “Darkwing Duck,” we felt that if we were going to do it, it had to be top, top-notch.

Are there other Disney shows from the ’80s and ’90s you’d love to bring back? I think of “TaleSpin,” “Gummi Bears” and “DuckTales.”

I always think of “Flight of the Navigator.” That was a Disney movie, I guess. I would never presume I’d do it, but that’s always been a movie I thought was cool. “Darkwing Duck,” though, I loved. And it’s very meta. It’s funny, I reread those “Calvin and Hobbes” comics recently and I realized they really formed a lot of my personality. Years ago, when we were first talking about doing “Darkwing Duck” again, I rewatched all of it and thought, this is really meta. It really breaks the fourth wall and comments on these shows I was also watching at the same time, at the same age.

If we can get “Gargoyles” back up and running …

That would be great. I did love “Gargoyles.”

Let’s talk about “The Studio” Season 2. There have been a lot of reports from the set: Madonna, the Venice Film Festival. Which real-life awards-season humiliation of yours is going to end up on the show?

How much does Variety figure into the new season?

I think it comes up. I don’t want to reveal too much, but some of the stuff has made it out publicly into the world a little bit. This idea of playing the awards game as a studio is definitely a theme explored throughout the season.

Do you have a Season 2 equivalent of the Martin Scorsese moment, when viewers see who’s appearing and think, “I can’t believe they got him?” Does Christopher Nolan show up, for example?

We have several of those. Some are really unbelievable, and having to direct these people has been among the most terrifying moments of my entire life. For ourselves, we really tried to be even more ambitious. We wanted to get people we were even bigger fans of and make them even bigger parts of the episodes, if we could. We also wanted to dig deeper into our own feelings about the industry and our own internal conflicts as we go about all this.

Does the awards race feel more or less relevant to you now? Having made “The Studio,” how does it look compared with 15 years ago?

What’s interesting is that until I did the “Steve Jobs” movie, which was pretty deep into my career, I was never part of anything that was on that journey in any capacity. I’d been to TIFF and South by Southwest to premiere things. But that was the first time I went to Telluride, and then we were in the New York Film Festival. Honestly, it was like a door to a secret part of the industry that I’d never been invited into was suddenly opened. So it’s interesting, because I had a very lovely career before any of this was even on my radar.

But that being said, the fact that “The Studio” won awards got us things in the second season that we probably wouldn’t have gotten in the first season. So there is some tangible outcome to some of this stuff. I understand why people get invested in it, and I understand the lure and the draw. I’ve seen people go on this journey and get the exact outcome they were hoping for, and it ultimately gave them none of the things they hoped it would. And I’ve seen people go on the journey and not get the outcome they wanted, and they had a good time and seemed to have good perspective at the end of all of it. It is a fascinating part of our industry to me.

I think especially for smaller things, it is incredibly helpful. It could make or break people’s careers. It could make or break a film. It could change the course of people’s lives. If you’ve already made many billion-dollar movies, winning best picture is a feather in your cap. It’s not going to change the course of your life, per se. But what’s interesting is those people are at these events right next to the people whose lives it will change. To me, that is really interesting to see in real life and really cool. For some people, they’re at the point of their career where awards have very personal stakes, but there are many other people here for whom the awards have real-life stakes. Will they get to do the thing they’ve always wanted to do, or will it not happen the way they hoped?

That is really interesting and scary and cool to see play out. There are those moments where your heart is pounding and you’re like, we’re doing it. This is what we asked for: to put ourselves out there and subject ourselves to reality in terms of how our work is being perceived. It can be very gratifying and incredibly scary and stressful.

Can you tell me something about “The Studio” Season 2? Is there a oner episode again?

We actually try to do much more of that. There are more episodes in a much more condensed timeline. I think there are technically several episodes this season that have no cuts in them, basically, throughout the entire thing. They’re real-time, half-hour moments in time that the episode is chronicling.

It’s a weird time in the industry. Depending on who you ask, the future looks very grim. Others say it’s an evolution and we’re just going through some changes. One of the biggest conversations here at Middleburg was Peter Rice going to Netflix. Someone like him, who’s been such a theatrical guy, making that move feels like a signal: Theatrical’s back! How do you feel about this moment? Do you get nervous, or do you think we’re going to be OK?

It’s a mixture of everything. It is everything at once. I’m very optimistic about some things. The fact that so many people are going to theaters, compared to the last few years, is so encouraging. I think we are finally getting over that hump of the pandemic and the strikes and all that. It seems like things are returning to a time when there are a lot of good movies and people are willing to go see them, and that’s really exciting. From my own personal lens, I can go to the theater on a Tuesday night and it’s packed and it wasn’t like that for a long time. As someone who loves going to the movies, it’s really fun to see. It reminds me of when I was a kid, honestly, a little bit more. And I think other things are terrifying.

“Sethical.” Friends from growing up still call me that when I see them. They don’t even think about it. It just comes out.

Something you loved as a kid but can’t believe you were into when you think about it now?

I get why people like “Magic: The Gathering,” but I spent every penny I had on “Magic: The Gathering” cards. That’s the thing I look back on, and I’m like, I should have bought other stuff.

I don’t karaoke as a rule. If karaoke went away altogether, I’d never need to be in a room with some drunk person screaming a song ever again. The rooms are getting smaller and smaller. Now I’m three feet away from this person. It used to be the bar was higher because you were subjecting yourself to a real big room full of people. Now you’re in a little room with just your friends in it, screaming your ass off like an idiot. It’s so loud. I hate it. That said, “All for Love” by Bryan Adams. If you have two other raspy-voiced friends, it’s a really good song.

I was going to say “The Apartment.” I would take “The Apartment.”

I’m pretty flexible. I can almost get my leg behind my head.

I just like vanilla. I did that movie with Barbra Streisand [”The Guilt Trip”], and she was obsessed with McConnell’s ice cream, which is from Santa Barbara. Every scene we shot, she’s like, “Wouldn’t we be eating ice cream in this scene?” So yes, it’s become McConnell’s.

My glasses come to mind. My shoes. Things like that.

What TV show or film in all of history do you wish you were a cast member of?

Maybe it would have been cool to be in “Ghostbusters” or something like that.

Which fictional character do you most relate to or admire?

I always liked Homer Simpson. Not that I relate to or admire him, but I always just liked him.

Your favorite piece of advice, either given or received?

I was told at a very young age to write what only I could write, which meant writing things based on my own experience, things that were happening to me. A stand-up comedian named Darryl Lenox, who’s passed away, unfortunately, told me that and he was really nice to me. I was writing jokes that were observational, like, “What’s the deal with crazy glue?” Those kinds of jokes. I was doing OK. I was maybe 15, maybe 14 and he pulled me aside and said, “Dude, you’re out there trying to get hand jobs and trying to buy beer and trying to sneak into parties and shit. No one else can talk about that. Talk about that. Don’t talk about fucking crazy glue. Any asshole can write that joke.” It was honestly the best creative advice I’ve ever gotten. I try to adhere to it to this day.

Welcome to the Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center at the California Science Center.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13).

After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour, sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall.

"It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.

"There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience."

Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life.

There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with.

As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top.

You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you).

This is the abbreviated description, but know that if you are visiting the California Science Center, you will want to budget a serious amount of time to explore all that this new center has to offer.

The new air and space center is designed for all ages, and for civilians and astronauts alike. For instance, looking at Endeavour spurred some memories for Reisman: He reflected on his time aboard the shuttle and his time as an astronaut and pinpointed specific places on the shuttle that played important roles in his mission.

"I'm looking at handrails that I held onto during a spacewalk," he said. "They're the same handrails. My hand was in the glove, but it was wrapped around those handrails. And I practiced for a long time exactly how I was going to do that, how I was going to root my tether, and all that kind of stuff. And I get to stand [here] now. When you go up the elevator there, you can actually have a direct view of those handrails, and every time I see that, I'm thinking about that spacewalk."

But you don't need to have completed a spacewalk to get that view. And, as of today, the general public is welcome to visit the museum, which is free to the public — as is the new aerospace center with its Endeavour exhibit.

However, due to the excitement over this new center opening, you will need to make a reservation online to attend. And, while the museum is free to the public, there is a cost associated with reserving slots during these busy first few days.

#680. Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk

A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

In a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version. The findings, published in the medical journal Neurology, suggest that the strength of a flu vaccine could matter for more than just protection against influenza.

The discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials. What began as a visit to discuss earlier vaccine research eventually led scientists to investigate whether different flu vaccine doses might be associated with different levels of Alzheimer's risk.

A Surprising Connection Between Flu Vaccines and Alzheimer's

Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and an increasingly serious public health concern. In 2025, more than 7 million Americans ages 65 and older were living with the disease, representing approximately 1 in 9 people in that age group. That figure is projected to more than double by 2050.

Researchers have been exploring whether common vaccines might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's. In a 2022 study, a team led by Paul Schulz, MD, found that flu vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's among adults 65 and older.

Schulz is a professor of neurology at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and director of the Neurocognitive Disorders Center at UTHealth Houston Neurosciences.

Three years after that earlier investigation, Schulz and his colleagues published new research examining a more specific question: Could receiving a stronger flu vaccine be associated with an even greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk?

The idea came from public health officials who had learned about the team's previous findings and invited Schulz to discuss them.

"The public health department had seen our vaccine research and asked if I could come down to talk to them about it," said Schulz, who is the senior author of the study and the Rick McCord Professor in Neurology and Umphrey Family Professor in Neurodegenerative Diseases at McGovern Medical School. "We went through the findings, and they asked if there was a difference with different dosages; I was confused."

Why Older Adults Receive Stronger Flu Shots

As people grow older, their immune systems gradually become less effective at recognizing and fighting infections. This age-related decline can make influenza particularly dangerous for seniors.

To help address that vulnerability, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends high-dose influenza vaccines as a preferred option for adults ages 65 and older. These vaccines contain four times as much influenza antigen as standard-dose shots. Antigens are the components of a vaccine that stimulate the immune system to recognize and defend against a virus.

The higher dose is designed to produce a stronger immune response in older adults, whose immune systems may respond less effectively to conventional vaccines.

Schulz had not previously realized that this stronger formulation was available.

"I was stunned that, as a physician, I didn't know a higher dose was offered," Schulz said.

Annual flu vaccination is recommended broadly, but preventing influenza is especially important for people with Alzheimer's disease. Flu infections and their complications can pose serious health risks for individuals already coping with cognitive impairment.

Before 2022, the CDC did not express a preference for one type of injectable influenza vaccine over another for people ages 65 and older. Instead, the guidance emphasized receiving a flu shot every year, regardless of the specific formulation.

Previous research from UTHealth Houston had already linked inactivated influenza vaccines, which use viruses that cannot cause influenza infection, to a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, researchers had not yet determined whether a higher vaccine dose might be associated with additional benefits.

Another practical issue made the question particularly relevant. As the population of older Americans continues to grow, demand for high-dose flu vaccines sometimes exceeds the available supply. Consequently, some seniors receive standard-dose vaccines instead.

This variation gave researchers an opportunity to compare Alzheimer's outcomes among older adults who had received different formulations.

"So we started looking, and sure enough, we were able to put together thousands and thousands of people over the age of 65 who got the high- or low-dose vaccine. They're more at risk for Alzheimer's than anybody else, of course, because it's age-related and we could look at high-dose versus low-dose and see if there was a difference," Schulz said.

Nearly 200,000 Adults Reveal a Significant Difference

To investigate the potential connection, the research team analyzed data from nearly 200,000 men and women ages 65 and older.

The results showed that people who received high-dose influenza vaccines had a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease than those who received the standard-dose formulation.

The researchers reported that standard-dose influenza vaccination was associated with a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk, while high-dose vaccination was linked to a reduction of nearly 55%.

The association was particularly pronounced among women, who appeared to experience a greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk with the stronger vaccine.

These findings add to growing evidence of a possible relationship between influenza vaccination and brain health. They also raise important questions about whether the immune response triggered by vaccination might influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's disease.

However, the findings demonstrate an association rather than establishing cause and effect. Additional research is needed to determine whether high-dose flu vaccination directly reduces the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's and to understand the mechanisms that might explain the connection.

What the Findings Could Mean for Alzheimer's Prevention

With Alzheimer's affecting millions of Americans and the number of cases expected to rise sharply in the coming decades, researchers are searching for practical ways to reduce risk.

The possibility that an existing vaccine could have benefits extending beyond influenza prevention is particularly intriguing. Unlike an entirely new treatment, flu vaccination is already widely used, and higher-dose formulations are specifically designed for older adults.

The new findings suggest that vaccine dosage could be an important consideration in future studies exploring the relationship between the immune system and Alzheimer's disease.

For now, the research provides another reason to investigate the potential benefits of influenza vaccination while emphasizing the need for further studies before drawing conclusions about Alzheimer's prevention.

Avram Samuel Bukhbinder, MD, a graduate of McGovern Medical School who is currently a clinical fellow in neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, served as a corresponding author of the study.

Schulz is also a faculty member of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center UTHealth Houston Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

Other contributors from McGovern Medical School included Elizabeth He, visiting scholar in the Department of Neurology; Kristofer Harris, MPH, research coordinator in the Department of Neurology; Mya Rodriguez, graduate research assistant in the Department of Neurology; Kamal Phelps, MD, an alumnus of the Department of Neurology; Jenna Thomas; Gabriela Cruz, MD, resident in the Department of Neurology; and Lauren Jhin.

Researchers from the McWilliams School of Biomedical Informatics at UTHealth Houston also participated. They included Xiaoqian Jiang, PhD, associate vice president for medical AI, chair of the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and Christopher Sarofim Family Professor in Biomedical Informatics and Bioengineering; Yejin Kim, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence; Luyao Chen, researcher; and Yaobin Ling, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow.

Materials provided by University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#679. Everything Trump has said about Jensen Huangs Nvidia saga

The company that makes the chips behind much of the AI we use every day is suddenly looking for a new CEO.

Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and ran it for 33 years, resigned Thursday after reports of two extramarital affairs: one was reportedly with a Nvidia executive who worked for him named Kimberly Powell, the other was with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom U.S. officials suspect of spying for Beijing.

Before all this, Trump and Huang knew each other pretty well. Huang was already one of Trump's tech advisers, and Nvidia had been asking the administration to let it sell more AI chips in China. When Trump invited Huang to Beijing at the last minute in May, the executive hopped aboard Air Force One during a fuel stop in Alaska.

When the allegations involving Alice Huang came up at Mar-a-Lago on Oct. 31, reporters asked whether Trump would keep Huang on as a tech adviser. Trump said he'd like to. "I’ve always found Jensen Huang to be very above board," he told reporters at his Florida resort on Halloween.

A little over a week later, on Nov. 8, reporters asked Trump again about Jensen Huang's future, this time at Nvidia. Earlier that day, Huang had apologized to employees in a bombshell email admitting he'd been unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia opened an investigation into whether he'd been targeted by foreign intelligence after reports of an affair with suspected spy Alice Huang. The board said at the time it had no reason to believe company secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised. Trump agreed, called Huang "an honorable guy." Did he think Huang should still run Nvidia? "I think so, oh yeah, sure."

Trump said he hadn't spoken to Huang about the allegations when he made those remarks. When he spoke to reporters again on Monday, Nov. 9, he said he'd asked Huang whether he knew about Alice Huang's alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Jensen Huang told the president he had no idea, according to Trump. "I really believe him," the president said. That left a question about what Trump himself knew. On Monday, Nov. 9, a reporter asked whether he'd heard about the allegations when he and Huang flew to Beijing in May. "No, I didn’t hear about it then," Trump said. The Washington Post reported on Thursday, Nov. 12, that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump about the alleged relationship aboard Air Force One on May 12, before Huang boarded in Alaska.

As new information from the New York Times and Reuters started coming out with reports that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, it became a little more difficult to maintain trust in the Nvidia boss — Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO and stepped down from the company's board.

Trump wasted little time pitching a replacement only a few hours later. He wrote on Truth Social:

NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! President DONALD J. TRUMP

For now, Nvidia's finance chief, Colette Kress, is running the company while the board looks for a permanent CEO.

As for Cook, he still has a job at Apple. He stayed on as executive chairman after stepping down as CEO in September, and neither he nor Apple immediately responded when Reuters asked about Trump's suggestion.

#678. Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed each year. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick. Antibiotics can treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may affect the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

Now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread. For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have tracked the complicated relationships among ticks, mice, oak trees, predators, and weather. Their research has uncovered unexpected patterns that could help predict when people face greater exposure to infected ticks.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries. The findings show how decades of observations can reveal connections that shorter studies might miss.

"On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk," said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the extensive data collected over the years have been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from coincidences and statistical fluctuations.

"Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare," said LaDeau. "This research has followed an ecological community -- including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms -- examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study."

Deer May Play a Smaller Role in Lyme Disease Risk Than Expected

When Lyme disease first gained recognition in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely driver of rising tick populations. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying numerous adult ticks, suggesting that areas with more deer might also produce more ticks.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. Although deer cannot pass the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks. Scientists suspected that larger deer populations would allow more female ticks to reproduce, eventually increasing the number of young ticks capable of spreading the infection.

But decades of monitoring have produced a different picture. On the Cary Institute's 2,000-acre forested research property in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant connection between deer numbers and the abundance of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks responsible for much of the Lyme disease transmission to humans.

"We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data," said Ostfeld, "but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing."

Mice Are a Much Stronger Predictor of Tick Surges

While deer populations failed to predict the abundance of nymphal ticks, mouse populations showed a much clearer relationship.

Years with especially large mouse populations were followed by approximately 40% more nymphal ticks the next year. White-footed mice are particularly important because they provide excellent blood meals for tick larvae and are highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to those feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can retain the bacteria as they develop into nymphs. When these nymphs take another blood meal, they can pass the infection to humans.

The findings suggest that tracking mouse populations could provide a valuable early warning of unusually high tick numbers.

How Acorns Can Predict Tick Populations Two Years Ahead

One of the most unexpected discoveries involves something that might seem entirely unrelated to Lyme disease: acorns.

Oak trees periodically produce exceptionally large crops of acorns in synchronized events known as acorn masting. These unusually productive years provide an abundance of food for forest rodents, allowing mouse populations to expand during the following year.

That increase in mice then supports larger numbers of young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly heavy acorn crop can reliably predict an increase in nymphal ticks two years later.

The relationship reveals a remarkable sequence of events in which the reproductive cycle of forest trees helps determine future tick abundance. It also offers researchers another potential tool for anticipating periods of greater Lyme disease exposure.

Why More Mice Don't Always Mean More Infected Ticks

Although mouse abundance helps predict how many nymphal ticks will appear, the researchers discovered that it does not consistently predict what percentage of those ticks will carry Lyme disease bacteria.

Initially, scientists expected both measures to rise together. Because mice are efficient transmitters of B. burgdorferi, an increase in mice seemed likely to produce not only more ticks but also a greater proportion of infected ticks.

Early observations appeared to support that idea. However, as additional years of data accumulated, the apparent relationship gradually disappeared.

"It kept me up at night," said Ostfeld, "because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong."

The explanation appears to involve the other animals that share the forest with mice. Skunks, squirrels, and opossums also serve as hosts for feeding ticks, but most are much less effective at passing the Lyme disease bacterium to them.

When these animals are abundant, more larval ticks may feed on hosts that are unlikely to infect them. This can reduce the percentage of nymphal ticks carrying the bacteria, even when mouse populations are high.

"So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts," explained Ostfeld. "It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case."

This finding highlights an important distinction between the total number of ticks in an environment and the proportion carrying the pathogen. Predicting the risk of infection requires understanding the broader community of animals that ticks feed on, not simply counting mice.

Extreme Heat and Cold May Not Kill Ticks in the Wild

Weather has also produced some unexpected results.

Earlier laboratory experiments suggested that exposure to intense heat or severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that ticks are surprisingly capable of surviving these conditions.

Researchers believe ticks protect themselves from temperature extremes by retreating into deeper soil layers or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less severe than at the surface.

However, the long-term data also revealed a more complicated relationship with temperature. Years that are warmer overall tend to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual, despite the ability of individual ticks to withstand short periods of extreme heat.

At the same time, warmer conditions generally favor mouse populations, which can lead to more ticks. These opposing effects make it difficult to predict how changing temperatures will ultimately influence Lyme disease risk.

What 35 Years of Research Mean for Lyme Disease Prevention

Taken together, the discoveries show that Lyme disease risk depends on a network of ecological interactions that is complicated but not entirely unpredictable.

Mouse abundance, for example, provides a stronger indicator of future nymphal tick numbers than deer abundance at the study site. Similarly, unusually harsh winters may not reduce tick populations as dramatically as previously expected.

By understanding these patterns, public health officials may be better equipped to anticipate periods of increased tick exposure and develop more effective prevention strategies.

Still, important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will affect ticks, the animals they feed on, and the oak trees that influence rodent populations.

"You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far," said Ostfeld. "We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it's very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production."

The research site in Dutchess County has undergone significant environmental changes since monitoring began in 1991. Climate shifts, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species have all altered the conditions in which the forest's plants and animals live.

Researchers intend to continue following these changes to determine how ticks and their hosts respond over time. Their work could provide increasingly valuable insights into how future environmental changes will influence human exposure to Lyme disease and other infections carried by ticks.

#677. Nvidia chaos, Dem sweep, lawsuits, protests: AIs terrible, no-good November

Investors and industry experts have long worried that the AI industry will expand until it inevitably bursts. And in the wake of a historic midterm election cycle that decidedly challenged the interests of Big Tech, the AI industry is facing enormous strain from all sides.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, a leading figure of the AI boom, has gone down in a salacious scandal involving extramarital affairs and accusations of Chinese espionage. SpaceXSI owner Elon Musk invested and lost millions on Republican campaigns during the midterms that he and other Big Tech leaders hoped would open up the floodgates to greater AI infrastructure. OpenAI and Anthropic have been implicated in numerous cybersecurity scandals on top of a domestic mental health crisis. Google, Meta, and OpenAI's ChatGPT are at the epicenter of a child safety reckoning that could change education and social media forever.

The latest challenge the industry is facing down is a lawsuit filed today (Nov. 12) by a safety and civil society groups Public Citizen, Irreplaceable Education Fund, Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI. The groups argue that AI's developers are aware of "imminent and catastrophic risks to humanity" posed by AI and urges courts to freeze the industry's development completely in the name of public safety.

"Despite endless warnings about the grave risks their products pose to public safety and even civilization itself, AI company executives are rushing to develop and deploy ever-more advanced AI systems," wrote Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, in a press release. "We the People should not simply stand by and tolerate AI executives’ unhinged risk-taking at the public’s expense. Our lawsuit asks the court to apply existing law and find the AI corporations’ reckless practices unlawful and freeze further AI development."

The group argues that companies are risking public safety by developing and releasing products they have admitted are potentially harmful, and that further development can be halted under California's Unfair Competition Law. In the first education-related lawsuit of its kind, a family is arguing their teen's access to AI on school-issued Chromebooks posed a life-threatening risk to her mental health.

Then on Nov. 11, a coalition of school and child safety groups led nationwide protests over Google's new controversy-stirring policies for schools. Advocates argue that Google's "ultimatum" presents an opportunity to pressure the tech giant into relinquishing some of its far-reaching AI goals. Many have urged districts to cancel contracts with the company and find AI-free alternatives.

Rocket Lab will launch its 100th space mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), and you can watch the milestone liftoff live.

An Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite is scheduled to launch from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site on Saturday, during a window that opens at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local time).

The mission, which Rocket Lab calls "The Mountain God Rises," will be the 100th to date for the California-based company. You can watch it live via Rocket Lab here, and Space.com will carry the feed if, as expected, it's made available. Coverage will begin about 30 minutes before launch.

Rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018.

In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers.

And it's hitting the century mark in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck.

"It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck said on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 launches."

Electron will meet the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery.

"Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab said via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage.

Not all of Rocket Lab's missions have gone orbital, it should be noted: A suborbital variant of Electron known as HASTE, which customers use to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment, has nine missions under its belt to date.

"The Mountain God Rises" will be Rocket Lab's 11th launch to date for the Tokyo-based company iQPS, which is building a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO. If all goes to plan, Electron's upper "kick stage" will deploy a single iQPS spacecraft 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth.

SAR satellites can see through cloud cover and image our planet at night as well as during the day, offering key advantages over spacecraft that are optimized to view in optical wavelengths.

#674. Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive

Mars may not be as geologically inactive as it appears. New evidence from mysterious gas emissions near an enormous Martian volcano suggests that heat and volcanic processes could still be present deep beneath the planet's surface.

Researchers have identified unusual concentrations of hydrogen chloride gas above fractures in the Alba Mons volcanic region. The findings suggest that gases from the planet's interior may be escaping through cracks in the surface, potentially revealing volcanic activity that has remained hidden until now.

An international team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy believes the gas could originate from hot magma underground. If confirmed, this would indicate that Mars still has dormant volcanic systems capable of releasing gases to the surface.

The European Space Agency's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first detected hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in findings reported in 2021. On Earth, hydrogen chloride is frequently released through openings connected to magma, raising the possibility that similar processes could be occurring on Mars.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," says Daniel Mège, Professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and co-lead author of the study published in Science Advances.

Mysterious Gas Emissions Defy Mars' Seasonal Pattern

The researchers noticed something unusual during early summer in the Martian northern hemisphere. Hydrogen chloride concentrations were unexpectedly elevated in a particular region, even though the gas normally becomes scarce at that time of year.

Hydrogen chloride levels on Mars generally follow a seasonal cycle. They typically peak during northern winter before declining to very low levels in summer. Scientists believe much of this behavior is associated with the planet's dust and water cycles.

However, the observations revealed a striking exception. Elevated hydrogen chloride repeatedly appeared in early summer over volcanic fractures on the slopes of Alba Mons. The unusual timing and consistent location suggested that something beyond ordinary atmospheric chemistry might be responsible.

Mars is home to the largest volcanoes in the Solar System, but scientists still do not know whether volcanic processes remain active beneath their surfaces.

Images taken from orbit indicate that some Martian volcanoes experienced eruptions within the past few million years. Instruments on the surface have also recorded marsquakes, demonstrating that the planet continues to experience seismic activity.

Together, these observations suggest that Mars may retain some of its geological energy. However, scientists have never directly observed a new volcanic eruption or fresh lava flow on the planet, leaving the question of present-day volcanism unresolved.

Fresh Cracks Reveal Clues to Hidden Volcanic Heat

To investigate the unusual gas concentrations, the research team combined atmospheric measurements with detailed observations of the Martian surface.

The Atmospheric Chemistry Suite aboard TGO uses infrared spectrometers to identify gases in the atmosphere. These instruments detected hydrogen chloride concentrated in a relatively small area shortly after the disappearance of winter frost.

Researchers then examined the same region using the orbiter's CaSSIS camera. The images revealed narrow fractures that appeared relatively fresh, with some extending hundreds of meters across the surface. Unusual changes in surface color were also visible around the cracks.

"The Trace Gas Orbiter was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," explains Daniel.

One possible explanation is that gases originating from magma deep underground travel upward through these fractures. On Earth, comparable volcanic openings are known as fumaroles.

The researchers propose that extremely cold Martian winters, when temperatures can fall to -120°C, allow ice to seal the fractures and temporarily prevent gases from escaping. As temperatures rise in early summer, the ice sublimates, changing directly into vapor and potentially opening pathways for underground gases to reach the atmosphere.

The discoloration observed around the fractures could also be significant. It may result from minerals or other substances deposited by escaping gases, similar to the deposits commonly found around fumaroles (volcanic gas vents) on Earth.

Although the connection between the gas emissions and volcanic fractures appeared promising, the researchers needed to rule out other explanations.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," concedes Daniel.

The team carefully evaluated the chemical reactions that could produce hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere, including processes unrelated to volcanism.

"A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food," adds Daniel.

After examining the atmospheric and geological evidence together, the researchers proposed that the gas could be escaping from a dormant magma chamber beneath Alba Mons. Such a chamber would form part of an underground volcanic system that could continue releasing gases even without producing visible eruptions.

Hidden Volcanic Activity Could Help Mars Support Life

The implications may extend beyond understanding the planet's geological history. Volcanic gases could also provide clues about how Mars evolved and whether it ever supported environments suitable for life.

In the distant past, gases released from magma, including hydrogen chloride, may have helped create a denser atmosphere and warmer conditions. Those conditions could have allowed liquid water to remain across large portions of the Martian surface.

Volcanic activity might also create habitable environments underground. If rising magma or lava comes into contact with groundwater, the interaction can produce warm hydrothermal systems. Such environments could provide both chemical energy and protection from the harsh conditions on the surface.

"Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," ponders Daniel.

Although the findings do not establish that Mars is currently erupting or that life exists beneath its surface, they offer an intriguing new reason to investigate the volcanic fractures around Alba Mons.

"These findings may prove to be TGO's greatest success yet," highlights Colin Wilson, ESA's project scientist for the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.
